name: Setmelanotide
lead: Setmelanotide, sold as Imcivree, is a melanocortin-4 receptor (MC4R) agonist given by daily subcutaneous injection. It was invented at Ipsen and developed by Rhythm Pharmaceuticals, and it is approved for obesity caused by rare genetic or acquired disorders of the leptin-melanocortin pathway [1][2]. It was approved in the United States in November 2020 and in the European Union in July 2021 and the FDA considers it first-in-class [1].

The current US label covers adults and children with acquired hypothalamic obesity (aged 4 and over) and with syndromic or monogenic obesity due to Bardet-Biedl syndrome or genetically confirmed POMC, PCSK1 or LEPR deficiency (aged 2 and over) [2]. It is not approved for ordinary polygenic obesity [1].

For people in the approved groups, the appearance chain runs through weight: the drug acts on appetite circuits and resting energy expenditure, most participants in the early one-year studies lost more than 10 percent of body weight, and reductions in body mass index were the primary outcome in a 2026 phase 3 trial in acquired hypothalamic obesity [1][4][5]. Outside those indications, safety and efficacy in people with common obesity are not well understood [1]. Setmelanotide is also a reference point in discussions of the melanocortin system, which regulates appetite and, in other receptor subtypes, skin pigmentation [10][15].

paras: The US label indicates setmelanotide to reduce excess body weight and maintain reduction long term in people with acquired hypothalamic obesity, Bardet-Biedl syndrome, or POMC, PCSK1 or LEPR deficiency confirmed by genetic testing [2]. An earlier approval described by Wikipedia covered the three monogenic conditions in people aged six and over, and notes it is not approved for variants classified benign, other genetic syndromes or common obesity [1].

There is no approved or studied appearance use. Wikipedia notes the drug has some efficacy in people without the approved genetic variants but that safety and efficacy in that wider population are not well understood [1].

Wikipedia describes two one-year studies, one in 10 people with POMC or PCSK1 deficiency and one in 11 with LEPR deficiency, all aged six or older; most participants lost more than 10 percent of their initial body weight after a year, and some reported less hunger [1][5]. A 2016 report described treatment of POMC deficiency with an MC4R agonist and a 2018 report described durable weight loss in three people with leptin receptor deficiency [8][9].

A randomized phase 3 trial of 14-week double-blind treatment followed by a 52-week open-label period enrolled people aged six and over with Bardet-Biedl or Alstrom syndrome and obesity at 12 sites in the USA, Canada, the UK, France and Spain; the primary endpoint was the proportion of participants aged 12 or older reaching at least a 10 percent bodyweight reduction at 52 weeks [3].

In acquired hypothalamic obesity, a phase 2 open-label trial and a 2026 phase 3 trial studied people aged four and over with a history of a hypothalamic tumour, lesion or injury. The phase 3 trial randomized participants 2:1 to setmelanotide or placebo for 52 weeks, with percent change in BMI as the primary endpoint and hunger score as a secondary endpoint [6][4]. The VENTURE trial examined children aged 2 to 5 [13]. A trial in Prader-Willi syndrome showed no benefit, according to Wikipedia [1][11].

Common effects include injection-site reactions, skin hyperpigmentation, headache and gastrointestinal effects [1]. The label lists disturbance in sexual arousal (spontaneous erections in males and sexual reactions in females, with an erection over four hours needing emergency care), depression and suicidal ideation, hypersensitivity, darkening of existing nevi and new nevi, and acute adrenal insufficiency in acquired hypothalamic obesity [2]. The label advises discontinuing during pregnancy unless benefits outweigh risks [2].

Setmelanotide is an MC4 receptor agonist with about 20-fold lower activity at MC3 and MC1 receptors. MC4 receptors in the hypothalamus regulate hunger, satiety and energy expenditure, and the drug is thought to restore pathway activity in people whose upstream signaling is impaired [2][1]. Unlike some earlier MC4 agonists it has not been found to raise heart rate or blood pressure [1]. It is a cyclic peptide [1]; reviews place it within the leptin-melanocortin pathway field [15][10].

Wikipedia adds that the drug also increases resting energy expenditure, and that a 2021 study in Science determined the structure of the drug bound to the MC4 receptor [1]. In people with POMC, PCSK1 or LEPR deficiency, the pathway upstream of the MC4 receptor is impaired, which is why a direct MC4 agonist is used [2][10].

Setmelanotide was invented at Ipsen under names including BIM-22493, RM-493 and IRC-022493, and Rhythm Pharmaceuticals developed it [1]. The FDA gave it orphan disease, breakthrough therapy and priority review designations and approved it for Rhythm in November 2020 as the first treatment for obesity due to POMC, PCSK1 or LEPR deficiency; the European Union followed in July 2021 [1]. Its first approval is reviewed in Drugs [12].

Later label expansions added Bardet-Biedl syndrome and acquired hypothalamic obesity and lowered the minimum age to as young as two years for some indications [2]. Wikipedia lists Health Canada as classifying it as prescription-only [1].

Wikipedia reports a 2021 US price of $330 for a 1 mg daily dose, roughly one day's treatment [1]. Because the drug is approved for rare, genetically defined conditions and carries an orphan designation, it is prescribed through specialist care. Setmelanotide appears in the wider coverage of obesity pharmacotherapy alongside GLP-1 drugs, and reviews place it within the leptin-melanocortin pathway field [10][15][16].

Human trials include POMC and LEPR deficiency phase 3 studies, a Bardet-Biedl/Alström phase 3 trial, MC4R deficiency work and acquired hypothalamic obesity trials from phase 2 to phase 3 [5][3][7][6][4]. Studies in children aged 2 to 5 and extension studies have also been reported [13][14]. No published trial has tested setmelanotide for facial appearance or in people with common obesity.

angle.text: Setmelanotide reduces weight in people whose obesity stems from defects in the leptin-melanocortin pathway, which can change body shape and appearance as weight falls. Its approved use is limited to defined rare conditions, so it is relevant to appearance mainly as an example of targeted obesity pharmacology [1][2].
